Learning Curve Collective
ECONOMICS • GRAPH REFERENCE

How to read any econ graph (the 10-second checklist)

1. Read the axes first. Half of graph confusion is assuming it's always P and Q. It isn't — check what's on each axis before anything else.

2. Movement vs. shift — the golden rule. If the thing that changed is on an axis, you move along the curve (endogenous — determined inside the graph). If it's not on an axis, the whole curve shifts (exogenous — it comes from outside). This one rule works on every graph below.

3. Then ask: what's the upshot? Every graph exists to make one point. Each card below tells you what that point is.

Color code: MICRO MACRO MICRO + MACRO ADVANCED MICRO

Tiles run in roughly the order the graphs show up in a course: intro foundations → AP Micro → AP Macro → advanced micro. Click any tile to jump to its full breakdown.

Where every econ course starts: scarcity, markets, and what happens when prices can't do their job. Graphs 1–10, in the order John met them.

1

Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF)

MICRO + MACRO
Y-AXIS One good (e.g. capital goods)
X-AXIS The other good (e.g. consumer goods)

What it shows. Every combination of two goods an economy can produce with its current resources and technology. Points on the curve are efficient, inside are inefficient (unemployed resources), outside are unattainable today.

The upshot: Scarcity forces trade-offs: producing more of one good means giving up some of the other. The slope is opportunity cost, and the bowed-out shape means opportunity cost rises as you specialize (resources aren't equally good at everything). A straight-line PPF means constant opportunity cost.
Movement along · endogenous

Moving along the curve is a choice about what to produce — you're re-allocating the same resources between the two goods.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • More/better resources (land, labor, capital) → shift out
  • Better technology → shift out (maybe only on one axis!)
  • Disaster, war, losing resources → shift in
  • Trade does not shift the PPF — it lets you consume beyond it
⚠ Watch out: A point inside the curve is unemployment/inefficiency — NOT a shift. Only resources or technology actually move the curve.
2

Supply & Demand (the market)

MICRO
Y-AXIS Price (P)
X-AXIS Quantity (Q)

What it shows. Demand slopes down (buyers want more at lower prices), supply slopes up (sellers offer more at higher prices). Where they cross is equilibrium: $Q_d = Q_s$ at price $P^*$.

The upshot: The price mechanism self-corrects. Above $P^*$ there's a surplus that pushes price down; below $P^*$ a shortage pushes price up. This one graph is the skeleton for half of econ — loanable funds, forex, labor markets, and AD–AS are all this graph wearing different costumes.
Movement along · endogenous

A change in the good's own price moves you along D or S (change in quantity demanded / supplied).

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Demand shifts: Tastes, Related goods' prices (substitutes/complements), Income, Buyers (number of), Expectations — "TRIBE"
  • Supply shifts: input costs, technology, number of sellers, taxes/subsidies, expectations
⚠ Watch out: "Price went up so demand fell" — no! Price changes cause movements ALONG demand. Only the TRIBE factors shift the whole curve.
3

Shifts vs. Movements (the #1 confusion)

MICRO
Y-AXIS Price (P)
X-AXIS Quantity (Q)

What it shows. The left panel shows demand shifting out vs. sliding along it; the right shows supply shifting when costs fall. The distinction is the single most-tested idea in intro econ.

The upshot: Ask one question: did the good's own price change, or did something else change? Own price → movement along the curve (endogenous — determined inside this graph). Anything else → the whole curve shifts (exogenous — comes from outside the graph).
Movement along · endogenous

Own price of the good. It's on the axis, so it can never shift the curve it belongs to.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Anything NOT on the axes: income, tastes, input costs, technology, expectations, other goods' prices, number of buyers/sellers
⚠ Watch out: A variable that is on an axis can only cause movements along; a variable not on an axis can only cause shifts. Check the axes first — this rule works for every graph on this sheet.
4

Consumer & Producer Surplus

MICRO
Y-AXIS Price (P)
X-AXIS Quantity (Q)

What it shows. Consumer surplus (CS) = the triangle between the demand curve and the price — value buyers get above what they paid. Producer surplus (PS) = the triangle between price and the supply curve — revenue above sellers' costs.

The upshot: CS + PS = total surplus, the economist's measuring stick for "how good is this outcome?" Free-market equilibrium maximizes total surplus — which is exactly why taxes, price controls, and monopolies create deadweight loss when they move Q away from $Q^*$.
Movement along · endogenous

Price changes re-slice the surplus: a lower price transfers surplus from producers to consumers and vice versa.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Any D or S shifter changes the size of both triangles
  • Policies (taxes, controls) shrink total surplus and create DWL
⚠ Watch out: Surplus is an area, not a point. For triangles: $\text{area} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \text{base} \cdot \text{height}$ — AP loves making you compute it.
5

Price Ceilings & Floors

MICRO
Y-AXIS Price (P)
X-AXIS Quantity (Q)

What it shows. A binding ceiling (e.g. rent control) sits BELOW equilibrium → $Q_d > Q_s$ = shortage. A binding floor (e.g. minimum wage) sits ABOVE equilibrium → $Q_s > Q_d$ = surplus.

The upshot: Price controls don't change what buyers want or sellers can produce — they just forbid the price from doing its rationing job, so the market can't clear. Quantity traded is the smaller of $Q_d$ and $Q_s$ (the short side wins).
Movement along · endogenous

Nothing moves along freely here — the control pins the price, and the gap between $Q_d$ and $Q_s$ at that price is the shortage/surplus.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • The government sets/changes the control level
  • D or S shifts can make a non-binding control become binding (or vice versa)
⚠ Watch out: Ceiling = below equilibrium to bind, floor = above. Students flip this constantly — remember a ceiling has to press DOWN on price, a floor holds it UP.
6

Elasticity (steep vs. flat demand)

MICRO
Y-AXIS Price (P)
X-AXIS Quantity (Q)

What it shows. How responsive quantity is to price: $E_d = \frac{\%\Delta Q}{\%\Delta P}$. Flat-ish demand = elastic ($|E|>1$, lots of substitutes, luxuries). Steep = inelastic ($|E|<1$, necessities, addictions, short time horizon).

The upshot: Elasticity decides who reacts and who pays. Inelastic demand → sellers can raise price and total revenue RISES; elastic → raising price kills revenue. It also determines tax incidence: the more inelastic side of the market eats more of a tax.
Movement along · endogenous

Elasticity is measured along the curve — and on a straight demand curve it changes as you slide: elastic up top, unit elastic in the middle, inelastic at the bottom.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • More substitutes available → more elastic
  • More time to adjust → more elastic
  • Bigger share of income → more elastic
  • Necessity vs. luxury
⚠ Watch out: Slope ≠ elasticity. Slope is $\Delta P/\Delta Q$ in units; elasticity uses percent changes, so it varies along a straight line.
7

Excise Tax & Deadweight Loss

MICRO
Y-AXIS Price (P)
X-AXIS Quantity (Q)

What it shows. A per-unit tax shifts S up by the tax. Buyers pay $P_c$, sellers keep $P_p$, the wedge between them is the tax. Government revenue = tax × $Q_{tax}$ (the shaded box); the triangle of trades that no longer happen is deadweight loss.

The upshot: Taxes shrink the market: $Q_{tax} < Q^*$. The lost surplus from those unmade trades is DWL — value that vanishes and goes to no one. Incidence doesn't depend on who legally pays: the more inelastic side bears more of the burden.
Movement along · endogenous

Given the tax, the new quantity is found where the vertical gap between D and S equals the tax.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • The tax itself (government policy) shifts S up by the tax (or D down, same result)
  • A subsidy is the mirror image: S shifts down, quantity over-expands
⚠ Watch out: DWL grows with the SQUARE of the tax (double the tax ≈ 4× the DWL) and is bigger when curves are more elastic.
8

Negative Externality (e.g. pollution)

MICRO
Y-AXIS Price / cost ($)
X-AXIS Quantity (Q)

What it shows. Production imposes costs on bystanders, so Marginal Social Cost sits ABOVE the supply curve: $MSC = MPC + MEC$. The market equilibrium ($S=D$) overshoots the social optimum ($MSC = MSB$).

The upshot: Markets overproduce goods with external costs because producers don't pay the full bill. The shaded triangle between $Q_{soc}$ and $Q_{mkt}$ is DWL. Fix: a Pigouvian tax equal to the MEC makes the polluter internalize the cost, shifting MPC up onto MSC.
Movement along · endogenous

Price/quantity settle where private (not social) curves cross — that's the whole problem.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Size of the external cost (MEC) sets the gap between MPC and MSC
  • Corrective (Pigouvian) tax shifts MPC up toward MSC
  • Regulation/quotas cap Q directly
⚠ Watch out: The DWL triangle points LEFT toward $Q_{soc}$, sitting between the two quantities. On the AP exam, always label $Q_{mkt}$ (from S = D) and $Q_{soc}$ (from MSC = MSB) explicitly.
9

Positive Externality (e.g. vaccines, education)

MICRO
Y-AXIS Price / benefit ($)
X-AXIS Quantity (Q)

What it shows. Consumption benefits bystanders, so Marginal Social Benefit sits ABOVE demand: $MSB = MPB + MEB$. Market equilibrium undershoots the optimum where $MSB = MSC$.

The upshot: Markets underproduce goods with spillover benefits — buyers only count their own benefit. The triangle between $Q_{mkt}$ and $Q_{soc}$ is potential surplus society never collects. Fix: a subsidy to buyers equal to the MEB.
Movement along · endogenous

Market settles at private curves' intersection; the social optimum is further right.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Size of the external benefit (MEB) sets the gap between MPB and MSB
  • Subsidies shift MPB up toward MSB (or S down)
  • Public provision (public schools)
⚠ Watch out: Negative externality → gap on the SUPPLY side (costs), overproduction. Positive externality → gap on the DEMAND side (benefits), underproduction. Keep the gap on the right curve.
10

International Trade & Tariffs

MICRO
Y-AXIS Price (P)
X-AXIS Quantity (Q)

What it shows. With free trade at world price $P_w$ (below autarky equilibrium), domestic quantity demanded exceeds domestic supply — the gap is imports. A tariff raises the effective price to $P_w + t$: domestic production rises, consumption falls, imports shrink.

The upshot: Trade lets consumers buy at the low world price — consumers win big, domestic producers lose some, and the country gains overall. A tariff claws surplus back to producers and government but creates two DWL triangles (overproduction + underconsumption). Total surplus falls.
Movement along · endogenous

Quantities respond along domestic D and S to whatever effective price rules the market.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • World price changes (global supply/demand)
  • Tariff or quota policy
  • A quota works like a tariff but the 'revenue' goes to license holders, not government
⚠ Watch out: Imports = $Q_d - Q_s$ at the world price — read it as a horizontal gap between the domestic curves, not a point.

Inside the firm: how production turns into costs, and how revenue and costs pick the profit-maximizing quantity. These four graphs are the toolkit every market-structure graph is built from.

11

Production Function: TP, MP, AP

MICRO
Y-AXIS Output (left: total; right: per unit of labor)
X-AXIS Labor (L), holding capital fixed

What it shows. Total product rises fast, then flattens as workers crowd fixed capital. Marginal product ($MP = \frac{\Delta TP}{\Delta L}$) rises, peaks, then falls — diminishing marginal returns. Average product ($AP = TP/L$) is pulled up when $MP > AP$ and down when $MP < AP$, so MP crosses AP at AP's max.

The upshot: Diminishing marginal returns in the SHORT RUN (at least one fixed input) is why marginal cost eventually rises — this graph is the mirror image of the cost curves. When each extra worker adds less output, each extra unit of output costs more labor.
Movement along · endogenous

Adding labor moves you along the curves.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • More capital or better technology shifts TP/MP/AP up
  • This is short-run: 'diminishing returns' ≠ 'returns to scale' (that's the long run, all inputs variable)
⚠ Watch out: Diminishing marginal returns starts where MP peaks, NOT where MP hits zero (that's where TP peaks).
12

Cost Curves: MC, ATC, AVC, AFC

MICRO
Y-AXIS Cost per unit ($)
X-AXIS Quantity (Q)

What it shows. $MC$ (cost of one more unit) falls then rises; $AVC$ and $ATC$ are U-shaped; $AFC = FC/Q$ only falls (fixed cost spread over more units). The gap between ATC and AVC is AFC, so they converge as Q grows.

The upshot: Two iron rules: (1) MC cuts both AVC and ATC exactly at their minimum points — when the marginal unit costs less than average, it drags the average down, and vice versa. (2) The firm's supply curve IS its MC curve (above min AVC). Every market-structure graph is built on these curves.
Movement along · endogenous

Producing more moves you along the curves.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Input prices (wages, materials) shift MC/AVC/ATC up or down
  • A change in FIXED cost shifts ATC and AFC only — MC and AVC don't move!
  • Technology shifts everything down
  • Per-unit taxes shift MC; lump-sum taxes shift only ATC
⚠ Watch out: Lump-sum (fixed) costs never touch MC — so they never change the profit-maximizing quantity. AP tests this trick constantly.
13

Demand, Marginal Revenue & Total Revenue

MICRO
Y-AXIS Top: price ($); bottom: total revenue ($)
X-AXIS Quantity (Q)

What it shows. For any firm facing a downward-sloping demand curve, MR lies below D with twice the slope (to sell one more unit you cut price on ALL units). TR = P×Q rises while demand is elastic, peaks where MR = 0 (unit elastic), and falls in the inelastic range.

The upshot: This links elasticity to revenue: cutting price raises TR only while demand is elastic. No profit-maximizing firm ever chooses to operate on the inelastic part of its demand curve — MR is negative there, so producing less would raise revenue AND cut costs.
Movement along · endogenous

Moving down the demand curve traces out the TR hump.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Anything that shifts demand shifts MR with it (same intercept, twice the slope for linear D)
  • For a PERFECTLY competitive firm, D is flat so P = MR — the TR line is straight
⚠ Watch out: MR < P whenever demand slopes down. If you see MR = P, you're in perfect competition.
14

TR, TC & the Profit Curve

MICRO
Y-AXIS Top: dollars; bottom: profit ($)
X-AXIS Quantity (Q)

What it shows. Profit is the vertical gap between TR and TC. The gap is biggest where the curves' slopes are equal — and slopes of TR and TC are exactly MR and MC. The bottom panel plots profit itself: negative at low Q (fixed costs), peaks at $Q^*$, falls again.

The upshot: This is WHY "produce where $MR = MC$" works: marginal quantities are just slopes of totals. If $MR > MC$, one more unit adds more revenue than cost → produce it. Stop exactly when they're equal.
Movement along · endogenous

Q is the firm's choice variable; profit responds along the curve.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Demand shifts move TR; input costs/technology move TC
  • Fixed costs shift TC up in parallel — the profit-max Q doesn't change, only the profit level
⚠ Watch out: MR = MC gives you the profit-maximizing quantity even when "profit" is negative — then it's the loss-MINIMIZING quantity (keep producing if $P > AVC$).

The four market structures plus factor markets and inequality. Same toolkit every time — what changes is the shape of the demand curve the firm faces and who has power.

15

Perfect Competition (side-by-side)

MICRO
Y-AXIS Price / cost ($)
X-AXIS Left: market Q; right: firm q

What it shows. The MARKET (S and D) sets $P^*$. Each identical firm is a price taker: its demand is a horizontal line at $P^* = MR = d$. The firm produces where $MC = MR$; profit per unit is $P - ATC$, so total profit is the rectangle $(P - ATC) \times q^*$.

The upshot: Short-run profit invites entry: new firms shift market S right, price falls, until $P = \text{min } ATC$ and economic profit is zero. Long-run equilibrium is productively efficient (min ATC) AND allocatively efficient ($P = MC$) — the benchmark every other structure is judged against.
Movement along · endogenous

The firm chooses q along its MC curve given the market price.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Market-level D or S shifts change $P^*$, which moves the firm's horizontal demand line up/down
  • Entry/exit shifts market supply in the long run (profits → entry, losses → exit)
⚠ Watch out: Draw TWO graphs side by side and connect the price with a dotted line. Shut down in the short run only if $P < \text{min } AVC$; exit long-run if $P < \text{min } ATC$.
16

Monopoly

MICRO
Y-AXIS Price / cost ($)
X-AXIS Quantity (Q)

What it shows. One seller faces the whole market demand, so MR lies below D. It produces $Q_m$ where $MR = MC$, then charges the price the demand curve allows at that quantity: $P_m$ (go UP from $Q_m$ to D). Profit = $(P_m - ATC)\times Q_m$.

The upshot: Compared to competition: higher price, lower quantity, DWL from the units between $Q_m$ and $Q_c$ where buyers valued the good above its marginal cost. Barriers to entry mean profit can persist in the long run — nobody can enter to compete it away.
Movement along · endogenous

The monopolist picks Q (and thus P) along fixed D/MR/MC curves.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Demand shifts move D and MR together
  • Cost changes shift MC/ATC
  • Regulation: forcing $P = MC$ (allocatively efficient, may cause losses for natural monopoly) or $P = ATC$ ("fair return", zero economic profit)
⚠ Watch out: Price does NOT come from the MR=MC intersection — that gives quantity only. Go up to the DEMAND curve for price. This is the single most common graphing error.
17

Monopolistic Competition (long run)

MICRO
Y-AXIS Price / cost ($)
X-AXIS Quantity (Q)

What it shows. Many firms with differentiated products: each faces its own slightly downward-sloping demand. Free entry erodes profit until demand is exactly TANGENT to ATC — price equals average cost, zero economic profit, at a quantity left of min ATC.

The upshot: Long-run: zero economic profit like perfect competition, but NOT efficient — $P > MC$ (allocative inefficiency) and the firm operates with excess capacity (left of min ATC). The inefficiency is the price of variety.
Movement along · endogenous

Firm picks Q where MR = MC, price from its demand curve.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Entry shifts each firm's demand LEFT (customers spread thinner); exit shifts it right
  • Advertising/differentiation shifts a firm's own demand out and makes it less elastic
⚠ Watch out: In the long run the tangency point is the giveaway: if D just touches ATC at the chosen Q, you're looking at monopolistic competition.
18

Oligopoly: Game Theory Payoff Matrix

MICRO
Y-AXIS (not a graph — a payoff table)
X-AXIS Each cell: (A's payoff, B's payoff)

What it shows. With few interdependent firms, each firm's best move depends on the rival's. A dominant strategy is best no matter what the other does. A Nash equilibrium is a cell where neither player wants to deviate unilaterally.

The upshot: In the classic prisoner's-dilemma pricing game, both firms cut price (Nash eq.) even though both would earn more by cooperating at high prices — individual incentives beat collusion. That's why cartels cheat and why collusion needs enforcement to survive.
Movement along · endogenous

Each firm's strategy choice, given the rival's choice.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • The payoff numbers themselves (costs, demand, fines, regulation) — change them and the equilibrium can move
  • Repetition: repeated games make cooperation easier to sustain
⚠ Watch out: Check for dominant strategies row by row and column by column, underlining best responses. The Nash equilibrium is where BOTH payoffs are underlined — don't just pick the cell with the biggest total.
19

Factor (Labor) Market — competitive

MICRO
Y-AXIS Wage (W)
X-AXIS Quantity of labor (L)

What it shows. Same side-by-side logic as perfect competition, but for hiring inputs. Market S and D for labor set $W^*$. The firm's demand for labor is $MRP = MP_L \times P$ (what an extra worker adds to revenue); it hires until $MRP = MFC = W^*$.

The upshot: Labor demand is DERIVED demand — it comes from the value of what workers produce. Wages track productivity and output prices. The firm's hiring rule $MRP = MFC$ is just MR = MC in the input market.
Movement along · endogenous

Wage changes move hiring along the MRP curve.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Labor demand shifts: output price P, productivity ($MP_L$: technology, capital, training)
  • Labor supply shifts: population, alternatives, preferences, immigration
⚠ Watch out: MRP falls because of diminishing marginal product — for a competitive output market it's $MP_L$ falling, not price.
20

Monopsony (single buyer of labor)

MICRO
Y-AXIS Wage (W)
X-AXIS Quantity of labor (L)

What it shows. One dominant employer (company town, some hospital systems). To hire one more worker it must raise the wage for ALL workers, so marginal factor cost lies ABOVE the labor supply curve. Hires $L_m$ where $MFC = MRP$, but pays the wage off the SUPPLY curve at $L_m$.

The upshot: Monopsony hires fewer workers at a lower wage than a competitive labor market ($W_m < W_c$, $L_m < L_c$). This is the one graph where a minimum wage (set between $W_m$ and $W_c$) can RAISE both wages and employment.
Movement along · endogenous

The employer chooses L along the given S/MFC/MRP curves.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Productivity or output price shifts MRP
  • Worker alternatives/mobility shift labor supply (and MFC with it)
  • Minimum wage flattens MFC up to the mandated wage
⚠ Watch out: Mirror image of monopoly: monopoly = price ABOVE marginal revenue point from demand; monopsony = wage BELOW the MFC=MRP point, read off supply. Wage comes from S, never from MFC.
21

Lorenz Curve & Gini Coefficient

MICRO
Y-AXIS Cumulative % of income
X-AXIS Cumulative % of households (poorest first)

What it shows. Plots what share of total income the poorest x% of households earn. Perfect equality is the 45° line; the more the Lorenz curve sags below it, the more unequal the distribution. $\text{Gini} = \frac{A}{A+B}$, where A is the sag area.

The upshot: One number summarizes an entire income distribution: Gini = 0 is perfect equality, 1 is one household earning everything. Taxes-and-transfers pull the after-tax Lorenz curve toward the 45° line; comparing before/after shows how redistributive policy is.
Movement along · endogenous

Reading along the curve: "the bottom 60% earn 30% of income."

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Progressive taxation & transfers → curve toward equality (Gini ↓)
  • Skill-biased tech change, returns to capital → Gini ↑
  • Measurement choice: income vs. wealth (wealth Ginis are much higher)
⚠ Watch out: The Lorenz curve must start at (0,0), end at (100,100), and can never cross above the 45° line. Cumulative means always increasing.

Zoom out: the whole economy on two axes. The business cycle is the story, AD–AS is the model, and the Phillips curve is the same model wearing different axes.

22

The Business Cycle

MACRO
Y-AXIS Real GDP
X-AXIS Time

What it shows. Actual GDP oscillates around a long-run growth trend: expansion → peak → recession/contraction → trough → expansion. The trend line is potential output (full-employment GDP) growing over time.

The upshot: Macro in one picture: the AD–AS model explains WHY we swing around the trend (demand and supply shocks), and stabilization policy tries to shrink the swings. Distance below trend ↔ recessionary gap; above ↔ inflationary gap.
Movement along · endogenous

Position in the cycle at a moment in time.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • The trend itself shifts with economic growth: resources, technology, productivity (same shifters as LRAS and the PPF)
  • Shocks (financial crises, pandemics, policy) drive the oscillations
⚠ Watch out: Recession = GDP falling (roughly two quarters), not just "GDP is low." A slowing growth rate is not yet a recession.
23

AD – SRAS – LRAS

MACRO
Y-AXIS Price level (PL)
X-AXIS Real GDP (Y)

What it shows. Aggregate demand slopes down (wealth, interest-rate, and net-export effects). Short-run aggregate supply slopes up (sticky input prices). LRAS is vertical at full-employment output $Y_f$ — in the long run, output depends on resources and technology, not the price level.

The upshot: The economy's master graph. Long-run equilibrium = all three curves through one point. Every macro shock is: which curve moved, which way, and what happens to PL and Y? (AD↓ → recession + lower PL; SRAS↓ → stagflation: lower Y AND higher PL.)
Movement along · endogenous

The price level adjusts to equate AD and SRAS; movements along AD/SRAS are responses to PL itself.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • AD = C + I + G + NX shifters: confidence, wealth, taxes, gov't spending, foreign income, monetary policy
  • SRAS: input prices (wages, oil), productivity, supply shocks, expected inflation
  • LRAS: resources, technology, human capital — same as the PPF shifting
⚠ Watch out: It LOOKS like supply and demand but the logic is different — the axes are economy-wide (PL, real GDP), and AD slopes down for macro reasons (not substitution/income effects for one good).
24

Recessionary & Inflationary Gaps

MACRO
Y-AXIS Price level (PL)
X-AXIS Real GDP (Y)

What it shows. Recessionary gap: short-run equilibrium (AD ∩ SRAS) left of LRAS → $Y_1 < Y_f$, unemployment above natural rate. Inflationary gap: equilibrium right of LRAS → $Y_1 > Y_f$, economy overheating.

The upshot: The gap tells policymakers which direction to push. Recessionary → expansionary fiscal (G↑, T↓) or monetary (rates↓) policy shifts AD right. Inflationary → contractionary policy shifts AD left. The gap is always measured horizontally: $Y_1$ vs $Y_f$.
Movement along · endogenous

Short-run equilibrium settles wherever AD and SRAS cross.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Whatever shifted AD or SRAS to open the gap (confidence collapse, spending boom, oil shock…)
  • Policy response shifts AD (fiscal/monetary) — or wait for self-correction via SRAS
⚠ Watch out: An economy CAN operate beyond $Y_f$ temporarily (overtime, deferred maintenance) — LRAS is sustainable capacity, not a physical wall. That's why inflationary gaps exist.
25

Long-Run Self-Correction

MACRO
Y-AXIS Price level (PL)
X-AXIS Real GDP (Y)

What it shows. Stuck in a recessionary gap, unemployment eventually drags nominal wages and input costs down → SRAS shifts right → economy returns to $Y_f$ at a LOWER price level, no policy needed. (Inflationary gaps self-correct the other way: wages rise, SRAS shifts left.)

The upshot: The classical answer to "do we need stimulus?": in the long run, no — flexible wages fix gaps automatically. The Keynesian rebuttal: wages are sticky downward, so self-correction from a recession can take painfully long ("in the long run we are all dead"). This debate IS the fiscal-policy debate.
Movement along · endogenous

Equilibrium slides as SRAS moves; the gap itself sets the pressure on wages.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Wage/input-price adjustment shifts SRAS (the self-correction mechanism)
  • Policy (shifting AD) is the impatient alternative
⚠ Watch out: Self-correction changes SRAS, never LRAS. Output returns to the same $Y_f$ — only the price level ends up different.
26

Phillips Curve (SR & LR)

MACRO
Y-AXIS Inflation rate (%)
X-AXIS Unemployment rate (%)

What it shows. Short-run trade-off: AD shocks move the economy ALONG the SRPC (inflation up, unemployment down, or vice versa). The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate $u^*$ — no lasting trade-off.

The upshot: The Phillips curve is AD–AS in different clothes: an AD boost = moving up-left along SRPC; a supply shock or a change in expected inflation SHIFTS the whole SRPC. In the long run expectations catch up, and unemployment returns to $u^*$ regardless of inflation — you can't buy permanently low unemployment with inflation.
Movement along · endogenous

AD-driven fluctuations = movements along the SRPC.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Expected inflation ↑ → SRPC shifts up/right
  • Adverse supply shocks (oil) → SRPC shifts up/right (stagflation: both bads rise)
  • Natural-rate changes (demographics, labor-market frictions) move the LRPC itself
⚠ Watch out: Map it mentally: AD shifts = movement ALONG SRPC; SRAS shifts = SHIFT of SRPC. Opposite of what students guess.

The financial plumbing: interest rates (nominal and real), how banks create money, and how currencies are priced. Watch which interest rate each graph uses.

27

Money Market (MS–MD)

MACRO
Y-AXIS Nominal interest rate (i)
X-AXIS Quantity of money

What it shows. Money demand slopes down (higher interest = higher opportunity cost of holding cash). Money supply is vertical — set by the central bank. Their intersection pins the short-run nominal interest rate.

The upshot: This is where monetary policy lives (in the classic AP framework): the Fed buys bonds → MS shifts right → i falls → investment and interest-sensitive consumption rise → AD shifts right. Chain: $MS\uparrow \Rightarrow i\downarrow \Rightarrow I\uparrow \Rightarrow AD\uparrow$.
Movement along · endogenous

The nominal rate adjusts to clear the market; movements along MD respond to i.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • MS: central-bank policy (open-market operations, reserve requirement, discount rate)
  • MD shifts: price level ↑ or real GDP ↑ → need more money for transactions → MD right; payment technology → MD left
⚠ Watch out: Money market uses the NOMINAL rate; loanable funds uses the REAL rate. Also MS is vertical because the Fed sets it — it does not depend on i.
28

Reserves Market / Policy Rate (new AP framework)

MACRO
Y-AXIS Policy rate (federal funds rate)
X-AXIS Quantity of reserves

What it shows. The updated AP Macro graph (post-2023): banks' demand for reserves slopes down, then goes flat at the interest rate the Fed pays on reserves (IORB). With AMPLE reserves, supply intersects the flat region — so the policy rate sits at the administered rate.

The upshot: Modern central banking doesn't ration reserves; it moves the policy rate by changing ADMINISTERED rates (IORB, ON RRP) directly. Small shifts in reserve supply don't change the rate at all — a key contrast with the old scarce-reserves/money-multiplier story.
Movement along · endogenous

With ample reserves, essentially nothing — that's the point: quantity changes don't move the rate on the flat region.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • The Fed changing IORB moves the whole floor (and the policy rate) up or down
  • Massive reserve drains could push supply back into the steep region (scarce reserves)
⚠ Watch out: If John's class uses the older curriculum, the MS–MD graph (#27) is what's tested; newer courses test this one. Know which story the question wants — they give different mechanisms for the same policy.
29

Money Creation & the Money Multiplier

MACRO
Y-AXIS New deposits per lending round ($)
X-AXIS Lending rounds

What it shows. A $100 deposit with a 20% reserve requirement: the bank lends $80, which gets re-deposited, $64 lent again… Each round shrinks by $(1-rr)$. Total new money converges to $\text{deposit} \times \frac{1}{rr} = \$100 \times 5 = \$500$.

The upshot: Banks create money by lending — the multiplier $\frac{1}{rr}$ is a geometric series cap, reached only if banks lend fully and no one holds cash. Real-world multipliers are smaller (excess reserves, cash leakage), which is partly why the ample-reserves framework replaced this story.
Movement along · endogenous

Each round's lending follows mechanically from the previous round's deposit.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Reserve requirement rr sets the multiplier
  • Banks holding excess reserves or people holding currency shrink the actual multiplier
⚠ Watch out: Only the FIRST deposit of new central-bank money creates the full multiplier chain. Moving existing deposits between banks creates nothing.
30

Market for Loanable Funds

MACRO
Y-AXIS Real interest rate (r)
X-AXIS Quantity of loanable funds

What it shows. Supply = saving (households, and gov't if in surplus); demand = borrowing for investment (firms, and gov't if in deficit). The REAL interest rate clears the market.

The upshot: This graph is where budget deficits bite: government borrowing shifts demand for funds right → r rises → private investment gets CROWDED OUT. It's also the long-run/real-side counterpart to the money market: saving behavior and investment demand, not the Fed, live here.
Movement along · endogenous

r adjusts; borrowing and saving respond along the curves.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Demand: investment opportunities/optimism, government deficits (borrowing)
  • Supply: private saving rates, foreign capital inflows, government surpluses, expectations
⚠ Watch out: Deficits can be drawn either as demand-for-funds shifting right (borrowing ↑) or supply shifting left (public saving ↓) — same result, r↑. Pick ONE, don't shift both. And remember: REAL rate here, NOMINAL in the money market.
31

Foreign Exchange Market

MACRO
Y-AXIS Price of the dollar (e.g. € per $)
X-AXIS Quantity of dollars

What it shows. Demand for dollars comes from foreigners buying U.S. exports and assets; supply of dollars comes from Americans buying imports and foreign assets. Equilibrium sets the exchange rate; e↑ = appreciation, e↓ = depreciation.

The upshot: Interest rates drive hot money: U.S. rates ↑ → foreign investors want dollar assets → demand for $ rises → dollar APPRECIATES → U.S. exports get pricier → NX falls. That's the exchange-rate channel that partially offsets contractionary-looking effects and links monetary policy to trade.
Movement along · endogenous

The exchange rate adjusts to clear the market.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Relative interest rates (capital flows)
  • Relative price levels/inflation (PPP pressure)
  • Relative income (imports rise with income → supply of your currency rises)
  • Tastes for foreign goods, speculation, central-bank intervention
⚠ Watch out: One country's currency demand is the other's supply — a single transaction appears on both sides. Always relabel axes for the currency in question, and remember appreciation HURTS that country's exports.

Intro-to-intermediate micro: put the consumer's choice under a microscope, then notice the firm's input choice is the exact same math. This is where econ starts feeling like one idea instead of forty graphs.

32

Total & Marginal Utility

ADVANCED MICRO
Y-AXIS Utility (utils)
X-AXIS Quantity consumed

What it shows. Total utility rises at a decreasing rate; marginal utility ($MU = \frac{\Delta TU}{\Delta Q}$) falls as you consume more — the third slice of pizza is worth less than the first. TU peaks exactly where MU hits zero.

The upshot: Diminishing MU is the microfoundation of downward-sloping demand. The consumer's optimization rule across goods: $\frac{MU_x}{p_x} = \frac{MU_y}{p_y}$ — equalize bang-per-buck. If good X gives more utility per dollar, buy more X (pushing its MU down) until the ratios equalize.
Movement along · endogenous

Consuming more moves you along TU and MU.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Preferences themselves (tastes changing reshapes the curves)
  • Utility is ordinal in modern micro — the curves' shape matters, the units don't
⚠ Watch out: Never consume past MU = 0 (TU falling), and with a budget, stop way earlier — where marginal utility per dollar is equalized across goods.
33

Budget Constraint

ADVANCED MICRO
Y-AXIS Good Y (units)
X-AXIS Good X (units)

What it shows. All bundles you can afford: $p_x x + p_y y \le I$. Intercepts are $I/p_x$ and $I/p_y$ (spend everything on one good); the slope is $-p_x/p_y$ — the market's exchange rate between the goods.

The upshot: Separates what you CAN do from what you WANT (that's the indifference curves). Income changes shift the line in/out in parallel (slope unchanged); a price change PIVOTS it around the other good's intercept (slope changes). This income-vs-price distinction powers the income/substitution decomposition later.
Movement along · endogenous

Choosing a bundle = picking a point on (or inside) the line.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Income I → parallel shift
  • $p_x$ or $p_y$ → pivot (one intercept moves)
  • Both prices and income scaling together → NOTHING moves (no money illusion)
⚠ Watch out: Doubling all prices AND income leaves the budget set identical — only relative prices and real income matter.
34

Indifference Curves & Consumer Optimum

ADVANCED MICRO
Y-AXIS Good Y
X-AXIS Good X

What it shows. Each curve = bundles giving equal utility; farther from the origin = better. Curves slope down, bow toward the origin (diminishing MRS), and can never cross. The slope is the marginal rate of substitution: $MRS = \frac{MU_x}{MU_y}$.

The upshot: The optimum is the tangency of the highest reachable indifference curve with the budget line: $MRS = \frac{p_x}{p_y}$ — your internal exchange rate equals the market's. If they differ, trading toward equality makes you better off. (This is the same condition as $MU_x/p_x = MU_y/p_y$, rearranged.)
Movement along · endogenous

Sliding along one curve = same utility, different mix.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Preferences shape the map (perfect substitutes → straight lines; perfect complements → L-shaped)
  • Budget changes (I, prices) move the tangency point
⚠ Watch out: Crossing indifference curves = contradiction (a bundle can't have two utility levels). And tangency fails for corner solutions — sometimes the best bundle is all-X or all-Y.
35

Income & Substitution Effects

ADVANCED MICRO
Y-AXIS Good Y
X-AXIS Good X

What it shows. When $p_x$ falls (BL1 → BL2), the move from A to C splits in two: A → B is the substitution effect (slide along the ORIGINAL curve to the new relative prices, using the hypothetical compensated budget line); B → C is the income effect (the price cut made you effectively richer).

The upshot: Substitution effect ALWAYS favors the cheaper good. Income effect goes the same way for normal goods, opposite for inferior goods — and if a good is so inferior that income effect overwhelms substitution, you get the (mostly theoretical) Giffen good with upward-sloping demand. This decomposition explains WHY demand slopes down.
Movement along · endogenous

The consumer re-optimizes; A, B, C are all tangency points.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • The price change itself, and whether the good is normal or inferior (direction of B → C)
⚠ Watch out: The compensated line is HYPOTHETICAL — parallel to the NEW budget line (new prices) but tangent to the OLD indifference curve. Draw it dashed; it's a thought experiment, not a real budget.
36

Edgeworth Box (exchange efficiency)

ADVANCED MICRO
Y-AXIS Good Y (A reads from bottom-left; B upside-down from top-right)
X-AXIS Good X (fixed totals of both goods)

What it shows. Two consumers, fixed total resources. A's indifference curves grow from the bottom-left origin, B's from the top-right (rotated 180°). Any point is an allocation of everything between them. Where their curves are TANGENT ($MRS_A = MRS_B$), no mutually beneficial trade remains — those points form the contract curve.

The upshot: Makes 'gains from trade' visible: from an endowment ω where the curves cross (not tangent), the lens between them is ALL the win-win trades. Trading inside the lens until tangency = Pareto efficiency. This is the baby version of the First Welfare Theorem: competitive markets land you on the contract curve.
Movement along · endogenous

Trades move the allocation inside the box (totals are fixed — it's pure exchange).

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • The endowment (who starts with what) determines WHICH efficient point you reach — efficiency ≠ equality
  • Total resources change = the box itself resizes
⚠ Watch out: Efficient (on the contract curve) does not mean fair — a corner where A has everything is Pareto efficient too. Efficiency and equity are separate questions.
37

Isoquants & Isocost Lines

ADVANCED MICRO
Y-AXIS Capital (K)
X-AXIS Labor (L)

What it shows. The producer's twin of indifference curves & budget lines. An isoquant = all (L, K) combos producing the same output; an isocost = all combos costing the same: $wL + rK = C$, slope $-w/r$. Cost-minimizing mix: isocost tangent to the isoquant → $MRTS = \frac{MP_L}{MP_K} = \frac{w}{r}$.

The upshot: Firms equalize bang-per-buck on inputs: $\frac{MP_L}{w} = \frac{MP_K}{r}$. If labor gets pricier, the tangency rolls toward capital — that's factor substitution (automation!) drawn as geometry. Connecting the tangencies as output scales up traces the expansion path, which generates the long-run cost curve.
Movement along · endogenous

Choosing an input mix along a given isoquant.

Shifts the curve · exogenous
  • Factor prices w, r → isocost slope pivots → different mix
  • Technology → isoquants shift toward the origin (same output, fewer inputs)
  • Target output level → which isoquant you're on
⚠ Watch out: Identical math to the consumer problem — swap $(x, y) \to (L, K)$, utility → output, income → cost, $p_x/p_y \to w/r$. Learn it once, use it twice.

Every shifter on one page. Remember the golden rule: these are all exogenous forces — none of them appear on the graph's own axes. If the variable that changed IS on an axis, it's a movement along, not a shift.

Micro: Demand — “TRIBE”

CurveShifts RIGHT / OUT when…Shifts LEFT / IN when…
DemandTastes shift toward the good · price of a Related substitute ↑ (or complement ↓) · Income ↑ (normal good; inferior goods flip) · more Buyers · Expect higher future pricesThe reverse of each — e.g. income ↑ shifts demand for inferior goods LEFT

Micro: Supply

CurveShifts RIGHT / OUT when…Shifts LEFT / IN when…
SupplyInput costs ↓ · technology ↑ · more sellers · subsidy · expect lower future pricesInput costs ↑ · per-unit tax · fewer sellers · expect higher future prices (hold back stock)

Micro: PPF & firm curves

CurveShifts RIGHT / OUT when…Shifts LEFT / IN when…
PPFMore resources · better technology · more capital/educationDisaster, war, losing resources (trade never shifts it)
MC / AVC / ATC(down =) input prices ↓, technology ↑, per-unit subsidy(up =) input prices ↑, per-unit tax. Lump-sum/fixed changes move ATC only — never MC
MRP (labor demand)Output price ↑ · productivity ↑ (capital, training, tech)Output price ↓ · productivity ↓

Macro: AD — “C + I + G + NX”

CurveShifts RIGHT / OUT when…Shifts LEFT / IN when…
ADConsumer/business confidence ↑ · wealth ↑ · taxes ↓ · gov't spending ↑ · foreign income ↑ · currency depreciates (NX↑) · expansionary monetary policy (i↓ → I↑)Confidence or wealth ↓ · taxes ↑ · G ↓ · rates ↑ · currency appreciates

Macro: SRAS & LRAS

CurveShifts RIGHT / OUT when…Shifts LEFT / IN when…
SRASInput prices (wages, energy) ↓ · productivity ↑ · favorable supply shock · expected inflation ↓Input prices ↑ · negative supply shock (oil spike) · expected inflation ↑
LRAS (= potential output = the PPF)More resources · technology ↑ · human capital ↑ · capital stock ↑Destruction/loss of resources; institutions collapsing
SRPC (Phillips)(shifts DOWN/left =) expected inflation ↓ · favorable supply shock(shifts UP/right =) expected inflation ↑ · adverse supply shock — note: AD changes move you ALONG, not shift

Macro: money & funds markets

CurveShifts RIGHT / OUT when…Shifts LEFT / IN when…
Money supply (MS)Fed buys bonds · reserve requirement ↓ · discount rate ↓Fed sells bonds · rr ↑ · discount rate ↑
Money demand (MD)Price level ↑ · real GDP ↑Payment tech (cards/apps) reduces cash need
S of loanable fundsSaving rates ↑ · foreign capital inflow · budget surplusSaving ↓ · capital flight
D for loanable fundsInvestment optimism ↑ · government deficit borrowingPessimism · balanced budgets
D for a currencyThat country's interest rates ↑ · its goods more popular · its price level relatively ↓Reverse — and remember its own imports shift the SUPPLY of its currency

Advanced micro

CurveShifts RIGHT / OUT when…Shifts LEFT / IN when…
Budget line(out =) income ↑ (parallel) · a price ↓ (pivot)(in =) income ↓ · a price ↑
Indifference curvesDon't shift with prices/income — they're preferences. Only tastes reshape the map.—
IsoquantsTechnology ↑ = same output with fewer inputs (curves move toward origin)—
Isocost line(out =) larger budget C · a factor price ↓ (pivot, slope −w/r changes)(in =) budget ↓ · factor price ↑
Exam instinct: when a question says "show the effect of X," first decide which market's graph it belongs on, then ask "is X on an axis?" If yes → movement along. If no → find X in the tables above and shift exactly ONE curve (two only if the question genuinely hits both sides).
